passage:
Trainee teacher's observation, week 3, Class 4C
I have been watching Parveen Ma'am's class for three weeks. She draws names from a steel tin to choose who answers, so the same confident children do not get every turn. Today the headmaster's nephew and Mridul, whose mother sells vegetables at the school gate, both forgot their homework. Both got exactly the same reminder and the same extra day.
Mridul noticed. At break he told me, "Ma'am doesn't have favourites. Even for me." Last week he sat at the back and never spoke. Today he moved to the second row and raised his hand twice.
I asked Parveen Ma'am about the tin. She said, "Fairness doesn't happen by itself. I have to choose it every day." I plan to use a tin in my own class.

qa.q: How does Parveen Ma'am choose who answers?
qa.a: She draws names from a steel tin.

qa.q: What does Mridul moving to the second row suggest about how he feels?
qa.a: He feels safe and valued, trusting that he will be treated like everyone else.

qa.q: What can other teachers learn from Parveen Ma'am's tin?
qa.a: That fairness needs a deliberate habit, so every child, not only the confident ones, gets a turn.

qa.q: How does Parveen Ma'am see fairness?
qa.a: As a choice she has to make every day, not something that happens by itself.

grounding: An observer's note shows a boy noticing that his teacher treats all children equally regardless of background, which makes him feel safe.

passage:
Wednesday
Something happened today that I keep thinking about. In the science quiz, Ishita, who always comes first and whose father is on the school committee, gave a wrong answer, and Joseph Sir said, "Not quite, try again," exactly the way he says it to me. Then when I mixed up a Hindi word, nobody laughed, because he never lets anyone laugh at mistakes, not even at Ishita's.
At my old school the teacher had favourites. I used to feel invisible there.
Here I feel safe to put my hand up, even with my accent. I answered three questions today!
I think Joseph Sir decides to be fair every morning. Like brushing his teeth.
Harish

qa.q: How many questions did Harish answer today?
qa.a: Three questions.

qa.q: How does Harish feel in Joseph Sir's class compared with the old school?
qa.a: Safe and confident, whereas at the old school Harish felt invisible.

qa.q: What does Joseph Sir do that makes the class fair?
qa.a: He responds to everyone's mistakes the same way and never lets anyone laugh at a mistake.

qa.q: How might Ishita experience Joseph Sir's fairness?
qa.a: She gets no special treatment, which might surprise her, but she is also protected from being laughed at.

grounding: A child notices a teacher treating all children the same whatever their background, feels safe, and sees fairness as a choice adults make.

passage:
Tuition centre note, Friday
Before class, one boy told a joke about Pooja's community, and several children laughed, Akash loudest. Pooja went quiet and stared at her book. I told the group firmly that jokes about anyone's religion or caste are not welcome here.
During the lesson Akash kept his head down and didn't finish his sums. Afterwards he waited till the others had gone. "I laughed," he said. "I don't even know why. Now I feel horrible."
I said that horrible feeling was his conscience working, and asked what he could do about it. He went straight to Pooja at the gate and said, "Sorry I laughed. It wasn't funny." She nodded. I also phoned the joking boy's parents that evening.

qa.q: Who laughed loudest at the joke?
qa.a: Akash.

qa.q: What was Akash feeling during the lesson?
qa.a: Guilty and horrible about laughing; he kept his head down and did not finish his sums.

qa.q: What did Akash do to make amends?
qa.a: He admitted it to the tuition teacher and apologised to Pooja at the gate.

qa.q: How might Pooja have felt when the group laughed?
qa.a: Hurt and alone; she went quiet and stared at her book.

grounding: A tutor's note shows a boy who laughed at a joke about a classmate's community feel guilty, listen to his conscience and apologise.

passage:
Monday
At lunch Kunal made a joke about people from Yamini's caste, and I laughed. Not a big laugh, but I did. Yamini was right there. She packed up her tiffin and walked off.
All evening I've felt sick. I kept seeing her face. Maa asked why I wasn't eating, so I told her. She didn't shout. She said, "That bad feeling is your conscience talking. Listen to it."
So I phoned Yamini (Maa got the number from her mother). I said, "I'm sorry I laughed. It wasn't funny and it wasn't true." There was a long pause. Then she said, "Okay. Thanks for saying it."
I'm not laughing at those jokes again. Next time I'll just say, "Not funny."
Chinmay

qa.q: What did Yamini do after the laugh?
qa.a: She packed up her tiffin and walked off.

qa.q: Why couldn't Chinmay eat that evening?
qa.a: Chinmay felt guilty and sick, remembering Yamini's face after the laugh.

qa.q: What did Chinmay do to put things right, and what is the plan for next time?
qa.a: Chinmay phoned Yamini to apologise, and next time plans to say "Not funny" instead of laughing.

qa.q: How did Yamini respond to the apology?
qa.a: After a long pause she accepted it and said thanks, which suggests she was still hurt but valued the apology.

grounding: A child who laughed at a caste joke feels guilty, recognises it as conscience and apologises, resolving to avoid such jokes.

passage:
Nature-club note, Saturday
On our walk to the old banyan behind the school, it began to rain. Most children ran for the shed. Damini stayed under the tree, head tilted back, watching water run down the hanging roots. "It's like a whole house," she whispered. "How old is it?" When I said it was probably older than all our grandparents put together, her eyes went wide.
Back in class she asked if we could plant "a baby one". I spoke to Deepak bhaiya, our gardener, and on Monday he will help her plant a neem sapling by the gate. She has already made a sign: "Growing. Please don't step."

qa.q: What will Damini plant on Monday?
qa.a: A neem sapling by the gate.

qa.q: What did Damini feel standing under the banyan in the rain?
qa.a: Amazed and full of wonder; she whispered that it was like a whole house.

qa.q: How did the nature-club leader turn Damini's wonder into action?
qa.a: They arranged with Deepak bhaiya for her to plant a neem sapling.

qa.q: How might Deepak bhaiya see Damini's sign?
qa.a: He would probably be touched that a child cares enough to protect the sapling.

grounding: A note shows a girl filled with wonder under a huge tree in the rain, which makes her want to plant a sapling.

passage:
Thursday
THE RAIN CAME. First the sky went purple-grey, then the wind shook the drumstick tree, and then drops as big as coins hit the dust. The whole courtyard smelled of wet clay. I stood out in it with my mouth open, and Vasudha didi laughed at me from the doorway.
Then I saw a long line of ants carrying eggs up the wall, all at once, as if someone had told them. How did they know? I watched for ages.
After the rain, Vasudha didi and I planted the mango seed I'd been saving, in the mud by the tap. I want it to be huge one day, so some kid can stand under it in the rain like me.
Nirmala

qa.q: What did the courtyard smell of?
qa.a: Wet clay.

qa.q: How did Nirmala feel standing in the rain?
qa.a: Amazed and delighted, standing with an open mouth.

qa.q: How did Nirmala's wonder turn into care for nature?
qa.a: Nirmala planted a saved mango seed with Vasudha didi after the rain.

qa.q: How might Vasudha didi see Nirmala standing in the rain?
qa.a: Vasudha didi found it funny and sweet, laughing from the doorway.

grounding: A child amazed by the first rain and a line of ants feels connected to nature and plants a seed.

passage:
Saturday
It was so hot today that the road looked wobbly. Under the parked car downstairs, a brown dog lay with its tongue hanging out, panting fast. I wanted to run and pet it. Lalremsiami said, "Wait, we don't know if it bites."
So I ran up and told Amma first. She came down with me and filled an old ice-cream tub with water. She said to put it down slowly and step back, and not to touch the dog. We did. The dog drank and drank, then licked its nose and wagged its tail once.
Tomorrow we'll fill it again. Lalremsiami is making a sign: WATER FOR DOGS, PLEASE DON'T MOVE.
I feel all warm inside.
Harsha

qa.q: What did Amma fill with water?
qa.a: An old ice-cream tub.

qa.q: How did Harsha feel after the dog drank?
qa.a: Warm inside and happy to have helped.

qa.q: Why was telling Amma first the right step?
qa.a: The dog was a stranger and might bite; Amma showed a safe way to help without touching it.

qa.q: How did Lalremsiami see the situation at first?
qa.a: Lalremsiami was cautious, warning that they did not know if the dog bites.

grounding: A child puts out water for a thirsty stray in the heat, checking with an adult first and helping safely.

passage:
By noon the village pond near Anirban's house had shrunk to cracked mud. A thin black dog was licking the damp edge, ribs showing.
Anirban and his friend Farhan stopped their cycles. "Poor thing," Farhan said. Anirban wanted to rush over with his water bottle, but the dog growled low when they came closer.
"Let's ask Dadu first," Anirban said.
Dadu came out with his stick and an old clay pot. "Thirsty dogs can snap. Put it there, by the tea stall, and step back."
They filled it from the hand pump. The dog waited until they were far away, then drank for a long time.
Farhan's father, who ran the tea stall, promised to refill it every afternoon. Anirban cycled home with a warm, full feeling in his chest.

qa.q: Where did they put the clay pot?
qa.a: By the tea stall.

qa.q: What did Anirban feel as he cycled home?
qa.a: A warm, full feeling of kindness and satisfaction in his chest.

qa.q: Why was asking Dadu first wise?
qa.a: The dog had growled, and Dadu showed a safe way to help without getting bitten.

qa.q: How might the dog have seen the boys at first?
qa.a: As a possible threat, so it growled and waited until they were far away before drinking.

grounding: A boy sees a thirsty stray dog in the heat and, after asking an adult, safely puts out water for it.

passage:
I'm Ramesh. Every Sunday Papa used to wash the scooter with the hose running the whole time, and my big brother Nilesh burned dry leaves and plastic bags together in the corner of the yard. The smoke stung my eyes, and after our water lesson at school, the running hose bothered me too.
I didn't want to sound like a teacher at home. So one Sunday I just filled a bucket and brought a mug. "Papa, can I try washing it this way? Like a race?"
Papa laughed but let me. It took one bucket, and the scooter still shone. The next week he used the bucket himself.
The plastic was harder. I told Nilesh the smoke hurt my eyes and asked if we could keep a bag for the kabadiwala instead. He grumbled, but he did it.

qa.q: How many buckets did it take to wash the scooter?
qa.a: One bucket.

qa.q: Why did Ramesh not want to lecture the family?
qa.a: Ramesh felt uneasy about the habits but was worried about sounding like a teacher and upsetting everyone.

qa.q: How did Ramesh suggest changes without shaming anyone?
qa.a: By turning bucket washing into a playful race, and by mentioning the stinging smoke and offering the kabadiwala bag.

qa.q: How might Papa have seen the bucket race?
qa.a: As harmless fun at first; then he saw it worked and switched to the bucket himself.

grounding: A child uneasy about the family wasting water and burning plastic suggests small changes politely without shaming anyone.

passage:
EVS teacher's note, Class 5B
For the water-audit homework, Tarun wrote that at home the kitchen tap runs through all the dish-washing and the garden hose is often left on. At the bottom he added, "I feel bad but I don't want Mummy to think I'm calling her wasteful."
I talked with him at break. We practised a kind way to say it: asking for help, not blaming. His classmate Maria helped him make a small card: "Can we try the bowl way this week? I'll help dry."
Today he reported that his mother laughed, tried washing with a bowl, and now has him count the buckets for the garden. He was beaming. I have asked him to share the card idea at Friday's assembly.

qa.q: What did Maria help Tarun make?
qa.a: A small card asking to try the bowl way.

qa.q: What was Tarun worried about?
qa.a: He felt bad about the waste but was worried Mummy would think he was calling her wasteful.

qa.q: How did the EVS teacher help Tarun raise the issue?
qa.a: They practised with him a kind way to ask for help instead of blaming.

qa.q: How did Tarun's mother respond to the card?
qa.a: She laughed, tried the bowl way and even got him counting buckets for the garden.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a boy uneasy about water waste at home who suggests a small change politely without shaming his parent.

passage:
The picnic at the lake was over, and the teacher shouted that the bus would leave in ten minutes. Chip packets and juice boxes lay everywhere under the trees. Uma pulled a plastic bag from her backpack and started picking them up.
"Look, Uma's the new sweeper!" Pallavi called. The girls around her giggled.
Uma's face burned. She wanted to drop the bag and run to the bus. But the ducks were already pecking at a shiny wrapper near the water.
She kept going, faster now, eyes on the ground. Five minutes left. Four.
Then someone crouched beside her. It was Pallavi's friend Sunaina, holding a juice box. "Where does this go?"
Uma held the bag open. By the time the horn honked, the bag was full, and two more girls had joined.

qa.q: What did Pallavi call Uma?
qa.a: The new sweeper.

qa.q: How did Uma feel when the girls giggled?
qa.a: Embarrassed; her face burned and she wanted to run to the bus.

qa.q: What kept Uma going despite the laughter?
qa.a: Seeing the ducks pecking at a shiny wrapper reminded her why it mattered.

qa.q: How might Pallavi see things once others joined Uma?
qa.a: She may feel her mockery fell flat, since even her own friend started helping.

grounding: A girl laughed at for picking up litter feels embarrassed but keeps going under time pressure, and others follow.

passage:
Every Sunday, before cricket in the colony park in Pune, Lokesh walked the boundary with a cloth bag, picking up wrappers and bottle caps. The ball kept getting lost in the rubbish, and the stray cows kept chewing plastic.
"Here comes the Kachra King!" Chaitanya shouted this Sunday, and the others laughed. Someone flicked a wrapper at Lokesh's feet. "Your majesty, you missed one."
Lokesh's ears went red. For a moment he thought of stuffing the bag behind a bench. Instead he picked up that wrapper too and kept walking.
The old watchman, Gopal Kaka, nodded at him from his stool. "Good work, beta."
And the next Sunday, when Lokesh arrived, Chaitanya's little brother was waiting at the gate with a bag of his own.

qa.q: What did Chaitanya call Lokesh?
qa.a: The Kachra King.

qa.q: What did Lokesh's red ears show?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed by the laughter, even thinking of hiding the bag.

qa.q: What did Lokesh do that showed quiet strength?
qa.a: He picked up the flicked wrapper too and kept walking instead of hiding or arguing.

qa.q: How might Chaitanya feel seeing his own little brother with a bag the next Sunday?
qa.a: Perhaps surprised and a little awkward, since his mockery did not stop others from following Lokesh.

grounding: A boy mocked for picking up litter feels embarrassed but keeps doing it, and others start to follow.

passage:
The power cut came at ten, in the middle of a heatwave, and the fan slowed to a stop. Jagdish lay sweating, thinking about the news clip from the evening: melting ice, burning forests, a reporter saying the planet was heating up. What if it kept getting hotter? What if there was no water when he grew up?
His chest felt tight. He tiptoed onto the terrace, where Nilesh Chacha was sleeping on a charpai under the stars.
"Chacha, is the world going to end?"
Chacha sat up. "That worry is real, and it's okay to feel it. Many clever people are working on this. And there are things you can do too."
"Like what?"
"Tomorrow we'll make a list. Switching off lights, planting trees, saving water. Small things add up."
Jagdish lay down beside him. The breeze was cooler up there.

qa.q: When did the power cut come?
qa.a: At ten, in the middle of a heatwave.

qa.q: What was Jagdish afraid of as he lay sweating?
qa.a: He was anxious that it would keep getting hotter and there would be no water when he grew up.

qa.q: How did Nilesh Chacha help with Jagdish's fear?
qa.a: He said the worry was okay, reminded him many people are working on it, and promised to list small steps together.

qa.q: How might Nilesh Chacha have felt being woken with that question?
qa.a: Concerned but calm, wanting to take Jagdish's fear seriously.

grounding: A boy anxious about climate change during a heatwave talks to an adult and is guided towards small steps within his control.

passage:
After the class project on climate change, Ujjwal couldn't stop thinking about it. At dinner in their Delhi flat he pushed his rajma around. "Mumma, the video said the seas will rise. Will Mumbai sink? Where will Nani live?"
Mumma put her spoon down. "You've been worrying about this all week, haven't you?"
He nodded. His stomach had been in a knot since Monday.
"It's a big problem, and it's okay to feel scared. But you don't have to carry the whole planet. Let's pick things we can actually do."
They made a list on the back of an envelope: cycle to school with Madhav from the next block, switch off the fan when leaving a room, start a balcony plant.
Ujjwal stuck it on the fridge. The knot loosened a little.

qa.q: Where did they write their list?
qa.a: On the back of an envelope.

qa.q: What was Ujjwal feeling since Monday?
qa.a: Anxious and scared, with a knot in his stomach.

qa.q: What did Mumma suggest instead of worrying about the whole planet?
qa.a: Picking small steps within their control, like cycling with Madhav, switching off the fan and growing a balcony plant.

qa.q: How does Mumma see Ujjwal's worry?
qa.a: As real and understandable, but too heavy for him to carry alone, so she turns it into small steps.

grounding: A boy anxious about climate change talks to his mother and focuses on small steps within his control.

passage:
The school trip to the paddy fields outside Thanjavur was nearly cancelled because of rain clouds, and halfway through, the sky opened. Bidisha and her class ran for the farmer's tin shed.
Karthik Anna, the farmer, stayed out in the field, knee-deep in mud, pressing the last seedlings into rows before the water rose too high. His back was bent and his shirt soaked.
"Why doesn't he come in?" Bidisha asked.
Their teacher said, "If the seedlings aren't in today, the crop could fail."
When he finally came in, dripping, Bidisha held out her towel. "Thank you for growing our rice," she said, feeling shy.
He laughed. "Eat every grain. That's thank you enough."
At lunch Bidisha scraped her tiffin clean and noticed how much rice other children were throwing away.

qa.q: What was Karthik Anna doing in the rain?
qa.a: Pressing the last seedlings into rows before the water rose too high.

qa.q: How did Bidisha feel holding out her towel?
qa.a: Shy, but full of respect and gratitude.

qa.q: How did Bidisha's new respect change her behaviour?
qa.a: She scraped her tiffin clean and noticed how much rice others were wasting.

qa.q: How does Karthik Anna see Bidisha's thank-you?
qa.a: He is amused and pleased, and asks only that she eat every grain.

grounding: A girl learns how hard a farmer works to grow her food, thanks him and starts wasting less.

passage:
Bidisha had never been awake at 5:30 before, but the exam made her. From her Kolkata balcony she saw a man in an orange vest sweeping the lane in long, steady strokes, lifting soggy leaves, broken glass and the paper cups from last night's puja stall.
Later she asked her friend Noor, whose Ammi knew everyone. "That's Shyamal Kaka," Noor said. "He does six lanes before we wake up."
Six lanes! Bidisha thought of the chip packet she had dropped from the balcony last week without a second thought. Her cheeks went warm.
The next morning both girls waited at the gate with a cup of tea. "Thank you for keeping our lane clean, Kaka," Bidisha said. He looked surprised, then smiled and took the cup with both hands. After that, Bidisha kept a small bag on the balcony for her rubbish.

qa.q: How many lanes does Shyamal Kaka sweep before the girls wake up?
qa.a: Six lanes.

qa.q: Why did Bidisha's cheeks go warm?
qa.a: She felt ashamed, remembering the chip packet she had dropped from the balcony.

qa.q: What did Bidisha change after learning about Shyamal Kaka?
qa.a: She thanked him with tea and started keeping a small bag on the balcony for her rubbish.

qa.q: How might Shyamal Kaka have felt when the girls brought tea?
qa.a: Surprised and touched; he smiled and took the cup with both hands.

grounding: A girl sees how a sweeper keeps her lane clean, thanks him and stops littering.

passage:
A huge brown dog had started sleeping by the gate of Hansa's colony in Jaipur. Every morning Hansa's legs went wobbly when she had to pass it on the way to the school van.
On Tuesday her friend Nandini picked up a stone. "Let's throw it. Then it'll run away."
"No!" Hansa grabbed her wrist. "It might get angry. And it's not doing anything."
She kept to the far side of the lane and walked slowly, not running, the way Papa had told her. That evening she asked the colony guard about the dog. "Oh, that's Sheru," he said. "Old and lazy. He just likes the warm step. Don't stare, don't run, and he won't bother you."
Hansa's heart still thumped near the gate. But now she knew his name, and it thumped a little less.

qa.q: What is the dog's name?
qa.a: Sheru.

qa.q: How did Hansa feel passing the dog each morning?
qa.a: Scared; her legs went wobbly.

qa.q: What did Hansa do that was wise?
qa.a: She stopped Nandini throwing a stone, kept her distance, walked slowly and asked the guard about the dog.

qa.q: What might have happened if Nandini had thrown the stone?
qa.a: Sheru might have become frightened or angry and snapped at someone, so the stone would have made things more dangerous.

grounding: A girl scared of a big dog keeps her distance, asks an adult about it and stops a friend from being cruel to it.

passage:
"Pooja! Snake! By the tulsi!"
"Where? Oh! Get the stick, I'll hit it!"
"No, don't go near! Nani says step back and call a grown-up."
"But it's scary!"
"I know. My whole body's shaking. That's why we stay far away." Charu grabbed Pooja's hand and backed towards the door. "Nanaji! Come quick!"
Nanaji came out, looked, and held up his hand. "Good girls. Stay on the step." He phoned the snake rescuer from the next village.
While they waited, Pooja whispered, "Is it going to bite us?"
"Not if we leave it alone," Charu whispered back. "It's probably more scared than us."
The rescuer arrived soon, lifted the snake into a sack with a hook and said, "Rat snake. Harmless. You were right not to hit it."

qa.q: Whom did Nanaji phone?
qa.a: The snake rescuer from the next village.

qa.q: How did Charu feel when she saw the snake?
qa.a: Very scared; her whole body was shaking.

qa.q: Why was Charu's choice better than hitting the snake?
qa.a: Stepping back and calling an adult kept them safe and did not hurt the snake, which turned out to be harmless.

qa.q: Why might Pooja have reacted differently from Charu?
qa.a: Pooja's fear made her want to attack it, while Charu remembered Nani's advice to keep away.

grounding: A girl scared of a snake keeps her distance and calls an adult instead of reacting with cruelty.

passage: Zainab, you're hiding your maths paper behind your back, and your face says the whole world knows. Sit with old Pranav Sir for a minute. When I was in Class 5, I got eleven out of fifty in arithmetic. I hid the report under my mattress and pretended to be sick for two days. I was sure every boy in class was whispering, "Pranav is stupid." On the third day my teacher, Iyer Sir, called me after class. He didn't scold. He spread my paper out and said, "Look. All your mistakes are in carrying over. Nothing else. This paper is telling you exactly what to practise." I practised carrying for three weeks. Next test, thirty-eight. So, show me your paper. Let's see what it's telling you.

qa.q: What mark did young Pranav get in arithmetic?
qa.a: Eleven out of fifty.

qa.q: Why did young Pranav hide the report under his mattress?
qa.a: He felt ashamed, sure every boy was whispering that he was stupid.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Pranav Sir's story?
qa.a: Iyer Sir showing that all the mistakes were in carrying over, which turned the failure into a clear plan to practise.

qa.q: How did Iyer Sir see Pranav's failed paper?
qa.a: Not as a label, but as information showing exactly what to practise.

grounding: An elder recalls feeling ashamed and hiding after failing a test, until a teacher showed him the paper was information about what to practise.

passage:
The science test came back with a red 9 out of 30, and it had to be signed by a parent by the next morning. Simran shoved it into her bag before anyone could see, but she was sure they all knew. At lunch she ate alone in a corner of the library.
Her friend Rukmini found her. "Everyone was talking about the cricket match, not your marks," she said. "What went wrong?"
Simran pulled the paper out. Together they looked. Nearly every lost mark was in the chapter on magnets, from the week she had been sick.
"So it's not you," Rukmini said. "It's magnets."
Mummy worked late shifts, and Simran waited up past ten for the signature. She showed Mummy the magnets pattern before she could even frown. "Can you help me with this chapter on Sunday?"
Mummy signed, and said yes.

qa.q: What mark did Simran get in the science test?
qa.a: 9 out of 30.

qa.q: Why did Simran eat alone in the library?
qa.a: She felt ashamed, sure that everyone knew she had failed.

qa.q: How did looking at the paper change things for Simran?
qa.a: It showed the lost marks were mostly in the magnets chapter, so the failure became a plan to practise.

qa.q: How might Mummy have felt when Simran showed her the pattern first?
qa.a: Probably relieved and proud that Simran had a plan, so she agreed to help instead of frowning.

grounding: A girl ashamed of failing a test learns with a friend's help that the paper shows what to practise, not what she is.
